[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Understanding Software Testing Types: Smoke, Sanity, Regression, and Re-testing"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In manual software testing, executing the right type of test at the right stage of the software development lifecycle (SDLC) is crucial for delivering a stable product. This tutorial explores four fundamental testing types: Smoke Testing, Sanity Testing, Regression Testing, and Re-testing."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Smoke Testing"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Smoke testing is performed after a new build is released to QA. It is a shallow and wide test designed to verify that the critical functionalities of the application work. If a smoke test fails, the build is rejected immediately, saving QA time."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Objective: Verify basic stability of the critical path."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Executed by: Both Developers and Testers."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Example: Checking if the login page loads, the user can log in, and the dashboard renders successfully."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Sanity Testing"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Sanity testing is a subset of regression testing performed after receiving a minor build with minor code changes (like a bug fix). It is deep and narrow, focusing strictly on the modified component to ensure the fix works without breaking adjacent features."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Objective: Verify a specific bug fix or minor feature change."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Executed by: Testers."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Example: Verifying that fixing a typo on the checkout button did not break the payment calculation logic."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Regression Testing"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"Regression testing ensures that new code changes, enhancements, or bug fixes have not adversely affected existing functionalities. It involves executing a broad suite of previously passed test cases."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Objective: Ensure overall system stability after modifications."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Executed by: Testers (often automated due to repetitive nature)."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Example: Re-testing user profile settings, cart operations, and search filters after integrating a new payment gateway."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Re-testing"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Re-testing is performed specifically to verify that a reported defect has been successfully resolved by the development team. Testers execute the exact steps that previously caused the failure."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Objective: Confirm a bug fix (Pass/Fail)."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Executed by: Testers."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Example: Defect ID 104 states 'Submit button is disabled on mobile view'. Retesting involves opening the app on mobile, filling the form, and checking if the button is clickable."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Differences Summary"},{"order":24,"type":"code","text":"Test Type       | Scope           | When to Execute                      | Primary Goal
----------------|-----------------|--------------------------------------|----------------------------------
Smoke Testing   | Wide & Shallow  | Build received from development      | Check critical system stability
Sanity Testing  | Narrow & Deep   | Minor build/fix received             | Verify specific component/fix
Regression      | Comprehensive   | Major releases or periodic intervals | Ensure no side effects from changes
Re-testing      | Targeted        | Immediately after bug fix            | Verify if a specific bug is fixed"},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"By understanding and properly applying these four testing types, manual testers can optimize testing cycles, reduce escaped defects, and ensure high software quality."}]
